title: Liberation theology
hookLine: Gustavo Gutiérrez read the gospel from the side of the poor

lines: HOW DO YOU SAY GOD LOVES YOU?
READ FROM THE SIDE OF THE POOR.
cards: In a poor neighborhood of Lima, in Peru, a Catholic priest named Gustavo Gutiérrez spent his days among families who had very little.
One question kept pressing on him: how do you tell people who are poor, and pushed aside, that God loves them? Not in theory. On their street, with their hunger.
Out of that question came a book, A Theology of Liberation, and a movement that came to share its name. Its starting point was simple to say: read the gospel from the side of the poor.

teach.b: Luke tells a scene in Nazareth.

Jesus stands up in the synagogue, unrolls the scroll of Isaiah, and reads words this path met earlier in Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor."
The reading goes on, all the way to "to set at liberty them that are bruised." Then he sits down and says this scripture is fulfilled today.
Gutiérrez asked: what does good news to the poor sound like to someone who is actually hungry? His answer had a few parts. First, God has a special love for the poor.
Not because they're better people, he insisted, but because God is good.
The phrase that grew up around this is the preferential option for the poor.
Second, theology comes second. First comes commitment: living alongside people and sharing their struggle. Then you reflect on it, in the light of the word of God.

Third, sin isn't only personal. It can be built into the way a society is arranged. Mary sings about God turning things over: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree."
Liberation theology drew both praise and criticism inside the Catholic Church, including from Rome, where some worried about political readings of the gospel and borrowings from Marxist analysis.
Its defenders answered that it was the gospel, read from a different chair. Christians weigh it differently.

teach.h: WHOSE EYES ARE YOU READING WITH?
teach.b: The question it leaves on the table is a plain one: whose eyes are you reading with?

how: In some Catholic and Protestant communities, small groups read the Bible together in light of their own lives and act on what they read; churches also speak of a preferential option for the poor in their social teaching.

games.q: you're in the synagogue at Nazareth, and the scroll of Isaiah is handed to you. which passage does Luke say Jesus reads?
o: good news to the poor, liberty for the bruised.
games.why: he reads the anointing to preach the gospel to the poor and set at liberty the bruised, then sits down and says it is fulfilled today.

practice: Bring to mind the story of the rich man and Lazarus: a poor man laid at a rich man's gate, covered in sores, hoping for crumbs from the table.

Now take Lazarus's place on the ground by the gate: what do you see from down there, who walks past, and what would good news sound like from that spot? If you pray, you can bring what you notice to God.

wordCard.voice: Liberation theology. Theology done from the side of the poor, starting with commitment, and reading the gospel as good news of freedom.

orig.note: Greek, Luke 4:18: release. the King James renders it "deliverance" to the captives and "liberty" for the bruised.
